brief.context: Japanese manga for a curious beginner
brief.subject: Japanese manga
brief.scope: History, genres, reading, industry, culture, getting started

node.label: Manga
node.summary: Manga is Japanese comic art, spanning every genre and age group, and a global cultural force.
node.hook: Japanese comics: a whole world of stories read back to front.

node.label: Origins & History
node.summary: Japanese sequential art evolved from scrolls and woodblock prints into a postwar mass medium.
node.hook: Manga has centuries of roots before Astro Boy.

node.label: Demographics & Genres
node.summary: Magazines target age and gender groups, which shapes genre and tone.
node.hook: Manga is sorted by who it is for, not just what it is about.

node.label: How to Read
node.summary: Manga follows Japanese reading order, which surprises new readers.
node.hook: Right to left, back to front.

node.label: Industry & Creation
node.summary: Manga is made through magazines, editors, assistants and collected volumes.
node.hook: Weekly deadlines shape the whole medium.

node.label: Culture & Adaptations
node.summary: Hits spill into anime, merchandise and global fandom.
node.hook: Manga drives anime, games and fashion.

node.label: Getting Started
node.summary: A few approachable series and sources make an easy start.
node.hook: Pick one story and you are in.

node.label: Edo-period precursors
node.summary: Woodblock sketches and picture books laid groundwork for visual storytelling.
node.hook: Hokusai coined the word manga.

node.label: Osamu Tezuka
node.summary: Tezuka created Astro Boy and introduced film-like pacing in the 1950s.
node.hook: The god of manga who made it cinematic.

node.label: Postwar boom
node.summary: Kashihon rental shops and weekly magazines turned manga into mass entertainment.
node.hook: Cheap rental books fed a hungry postwar audience.

node.label: Global spread
node.summary: Translations in the 1990s and 2000s made manga a worldwide publishing category.
node.hook: From Tokyo bookshelves to every continent.

node.label: Shonen
node.summary: Targets teen boys; examples include One Piece and Naruto.
node.hook: Fighting, friendship and never giving up.

text: Demographic labels like shonen and seinen describe audience, not content, so genres cross them.

node.label: Shojo
node.summary: Targets teen girls; examples include Sailor Moon and Fruits Basket.
node.hook: Romance and emotion drive the story.

node.label: Seinen
node.summary: Targets adult men; examples include Berserk and Vinland Saga.
node.hook: Darker, more mature storytelling.

node.label: Josei
node.summary: Focuses on relationships and daily life, as in Nana.
node.hook: Realistic stories for adult women.

node.label: Isekai
node.summary: A hugely popular genre where the hero is transported to a fantasy realm.
node.hook: Ordinary person, another world.

node.label: Slice of life
node.summary: Everyday stories with low stakes and strong atmosphere, like Yotsuba&!.
node.hook: Quiet days, big feelings.

node.label: Right-to-left order
node.summary: Pages and panels flow right to left; most English editions preserve this.
node.hook: Start at the back cover.

node.label: Sound effects
node.summary: Drawn sound words add atmosphere and are often kept or translated in the margins.
node.hook: Onomatopoeia is part of the art.

node.label: Panel flow
node.summary: Panel size and shape control pacing; big panels slow down, narrow ones speed up.
node.hook: Panels guide your eye like a map.

node.label: Mangaka and editors
node.summary: Authors work with an editor and assistants to meet strict schedules.
node.hook: The artist writes and draws; the editor steers.

node.label: Serialization
node.summary: Popular series get collected as tankobon volumes.
node.hook: Chapters appear weekly or monthly in magazines.

node.label: Assistants and studios
node.summary: Assistants handle inking, screentone and backgrounds to meet deadlines.
node.hook: Backgrounds are often drawn by a team.

node.label: Weekly Shonen Jump
node.summary: Shueisha magazine behind Dragon Ball, One Piece and My Hero Academia.
node.hook: The magazine that launched a thousand heroes.

node.label: Anime adaptations
node.summary: Adaptations expand reach but may diverge from the source.
node.hook: Popular manga become TV shows and films.

node.label: Fan translations and scanlation
node.summary: Unlicensed translations grew the audience and pushed official releases.
node.hook: Fans spread it first; publishers followed.

node.label: Cosplay and conventions
node.summary: Events worldwide celebrate manga through costumes and meetups.
node.hook: Fans become the characters.

node.label: Merchandise
node.summary: Licensed goods are a major revenue stream alongside the books.
node.hook: Figures, keychains and everything in between.

node.label: Starter series
node.summary: Try Fullmetal Alchemist, Death Note or Spy x Family.
node.hook: Short and finished beats long and sprawling.

node.label: Where to read
node.summary: Apps like Manga Plus and Viz, and print volumes, offer licensed reading.
node.hook: Legal options are plentiful.

node.label: Buying volumes
node.summary: Collected volumes are widely sold in bookshops and online.
node.hook: Tankobon volumes make a great shelf.

node.label: Libraries
node.summary: Many public libraries stock manga, letting you try series before buying.
node.hook: Free and a great way to sample.

edge.why: Tezuka shaped the serial story format.
Jump is the flagship shonen magazine.
Some starters like Death Note are seinen.
Check reading direction when buying volumes.
Fan demand pushed official digital release.
Early picture books developed the visual language.

text: Weekly serialization is the engine behind both manga pacing and anime adaptations.
